title: Do a Legislator's Trades Anticipate Legislative Acts? Timing, Disclosure and Proximity Tests on the STOCK Act Filings of the Pelosi Household, 2014–2026
abstract: The trades disclosed under the STOCK Act by the household of Representative Nancy Pelosi are widely presented as evidence that a legislator can anticipate acts of Congress and beat the market. This paper tests the claim with three event-study designs on the complete record of 65 Periodic Transaction Reports filed between 2014 and 2026 (227 transactions, 117 discretionary events after cleaning, 68 involving long call options). First, timing: signed abnormal returns after the trades are nil at 5, 20 and 60 sessions; over one year purchases beat the S&P 500 by 15.9 per cent but the Nasdaq-100 by 12.2, and the stocks sold went on to outperform by 24.5 per cent, so that purchases and sales together earn nothing against either benchmark. Second, disclosure: no abnormal volume or return when the filings become public, including in 2021–2026 when aggregators publish them within hours. Third, proximity: of 88 act–ticker pairs built from 42 federal acts affecting the traded stocks (votes, enactments, AI-chip export controls, antitrust actions), 3 were preceded within 60 days by a trade in the expected direction, against 4.4 expected under random dates, and 8 by a trade in the opposite direction. The household buys after declines and holds a leveraged, concentrated position in large-cap technology through a bull market; the record contains no trace of informed timing. A base-rate rule follows: with ten trades a year on a dozen tickers that are the object of federal action several times a year, coincidence is the null hypothesis, not the finding.
why: Rigorous negative result: legislator trades beat no benchmark, updates prior.

title: From Backtest to Deployment: A Staged-capital Protocol for Evaluating Agentic Trading Systems - A Position Paper Proposing an Engineering Workflow for Committing Real Capital to Autonomous Trading Agents
abstract: Existing critiques of backtested alpha in agentic trading systems correctly diagnose the problem-lookahead bias, interface-driven behavior, absence of stable directional edge-but stop short of prescribing what a practitioner should do before committing capital. Reporting standards such as the P1-P6 protocol evaluate a claim after the fact; they do not tell an engineer when or how to move a system from backtest to live capital. This paper proposes a staged-capital evaluation protocol: zero-weight shadow validation, forward paper-testing on live data, minimal live capital gated by deterministic and mechanical exit logic, and gradual scaling gated by pre-registered statistical tests. We ground the protocol's central design choice-that exit and sizing logic must be mechanical rather than modelmediated-in production evidence showing that forcing an agent to self-report risk exposure before entry changed none of its behavior, and that a fixed mechanical stop/target bracket outperformed discretionary exits. We corroborate the shadow-validation stage with an independent engineering observation from a real institutional deployment. We conclude that the missing piece in agentic trading evaluation is not more reporting theory but a deployable, falsifiable rollout protocol.
why: Position paper but directly addresses backtest-to-live validation gap.

title: From Hindsight to Foresight: Adapting Reusable Reasoning Structures from Recurring Financial Events
abstract: Forecasting real-world events requires reasoning under uncertainty from information available at a fixed cutoff. Recent work has improved how large language models (LLMs) retrieve evidence and produce probabilistic forecasts, but each question is treated independently even when similar events recur. Resolved occurrences carry experience for later forecasts, yet past outcomes and case summaries do not preserve the relationships that made an earlier occurrence informative. We develop ReFoRM (Recurrent-event Forecasting with Reasoning Memory), which organizes reasoning from resolved events into predictive paths, retrieves relevant paths for a later occurrence, and reconstructs their relations using evidence at the new forecast cutoff. We evaluate ReFoRM on the Recurring Financial Events Set, which contains 300 questions across 40 recurring financial event families and uses earlier occurrences as hindsight for 100 forecast targets. Across five LLMs and six baselines, ReFoRM improves categorical and probabilistic forecasting performance. Further analyses show that validating historical relations with current evidence and reconstructing them enhances forecasting. Reasoning evaluation also demonstrates stronger evidence grounding, logical validity, and mechanism specificity.
why: LLMs forecast recurring financial events with named dataset, concrete method.

title: Fedspeak, LLM-Derived Signals, and High-Frequency Trading
abstract: Financial markets are often assumed to incorporate Federal Reserve policy decisions instantaneously. Yet it remains unclear whether markets fully absorb policy-relevant information at the moment of release, or whether information continues to be revealed as the policy narrative unfolds across sequential communications. I construct a novel measure of policy communication shocks, the Communication Divergence Signal (CDS), which captures semantic, tonal, and framing shifts across sequential FOMC communications. Using large language models and high-frequency event-study methods, I show that communication divergence generates significant and persistent movements in intraday asset prices and abnormal trading volume. Abnormal trading volume is measured relative to non-announcement benchmarks at the same intraday horizon, isolating excess trading activity associated with information arrival. I further document systematic responses in daily open interest, consistent with belief updating and position reallocation rather than transitory liquidity provision. These findings highlight the role of communication sequencing and framing in shaping price discovery and trading dynamics across financial markets.
why: LLM Fed signals tested on real HF market data, actionable.

title: NeuroLedger-GTX: A Temporal Graph-Transformer with Attention-Gated Conformal Risk Control for Real-Time Fraud and Anti-Money-Laundering Detection in Retail and Corporate Banking
abstract: Retail and corporate banking rails process millions of debit, credit, wire, and real-time payment orders every day. A small share of that flow is fraudulent or used to move illicit funds, and analysts need a single ranked queue that respects a fixed daily budget, keeps its probability meaningful across drift, and holds up when a counterparty actively camouflages a transfer. Existing production stacks split these needs across three components that rarely share a decision layer. This paper presents NeuroLedger-GTX, a framework that combines a Temporal Graph Transformer over a rolling transaction neighborhood, a heterogeneous account graph neural network over the aggregated transfer graph, a graph-anchored fusion module, and an Attention-Gated Conformal Layer that adapts thresholds to both the payment channel and to the model's own attention-weighted context richness. Using a synthetic banking ledger of 90,000 transactions across 15,000 accounts and twelve monthly windows, the framework reaches AUROC 0.729 for fraud and 0.764 for anti-money laundering on an out-of-time evaluation, with recall 0.868 at the conformal decision point for fraud and 0.854 for anti-money laundering. Under a camouflage attack that rewrites amounts below reporting thresholds, disguises timing, swaps merchant category, and clears sender risk flags, a standard gradient-boosted model loses 0.262 AUROC while NeuroLedger-GTX loses 0.139. The paper also reports segment breakdowns, calibration diagnostics, an alert-budget cost curve, and a rolling AUROC over the year. A supplementary bundle ships the data generator, model code, training log, and results. The paper is written as a self-contained record of the framework, not as a call for further experimentation.
why: Fraud detection solid but on synthetic data, not core focus.

title: Structural Imbalances in the Generative AI Market: Inference Unit Economics, the Aggregate CapEx-Revenue Gap, and a Stylized Liquidity-Depletion Model
abstract: This working paper develops a quantitative accounting framework for assessing the internal consistency of the capital-formation cycle in the generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) and large language model (LLM) industry as of 2026. Three components are formalised. First, a bottom-up engineering cost model for the inference of frontier ultra-large models (parameter counts of the order of 2.8 × 10 12) is used to bound the implied gap between the marginal compute cost and observed end-user prices; under unbatched single-stream execution the implied cost-to-revenue ratio reaches approximately 3,950×, which falls to a range of roughly 30×-100× once dynamic batching and low-precision quantisation are accounted for. Second, a two-equation exponential divergence model of infrastructure capital expenditure and end-market AI revenue is calibrated on 2023-2026 public disclosures and third-party estimates, yielding an implied annual funding gap in excess of USD 600 billion. Third, an efficiency-adjusted demand identity is derived, showing that when the growth rate of tokens-per-accelerator efficiency exceeds the growth rate of token demand, net physical accelerator demand contracts-a mechanism we label the inverted Jevons regime. These components are combined with a Cash Flow-to-CapEx Sustainability Ratio (CFSR) and with publicly disclosed intra-ecosystem investment and procurement commitments to characterise the conditions under which the observed expenditure trajectory ceases to be organically fundable. A stylized, deliberately non-firm-specific liquidity-depletion model illustrates the timing of the transition to external financing dependence. The paper concludes with a set of falsifiable predictions, a discussion of alternative hypotheses under which no repricing occurs, and implications for financial-stability monitoring and corporate disclosure. The paper is an analytical exercise in industrial and financial economics; it contains no investment recommendation.
why: Solid AI economics analysis; not actionable for traders.

title: When Demand Feeds Supply: Circular Finance and Welfare in AIEcosystems
abstract: AI compute markets combine supplier finance with commitments to purchase capacity. We showthat the same commitment can expand usable computing capacity yet reduce welfare when it causesusers and financiers to infer more underlying demand than the capacity can support. In a two-periodmodel, perceived demand attracts continuation finance and amplifies this mismatch when that financeresponds strongly to the signal. Private incentives can therefore generate excessive commitments evenwhen finance relaxes a real compute constraint. Welfare-improving regulation can combine provenanceseparation with a levy on signal rents, while productive finance may instead merit a subsidy. Two sourcedocumentedAI infrastructure cases motivate the mechanism.
why: Theory with documented cases, mechanism interesting but not actionable.

title: Does the Model Matter? A Sensitivity Analysis of Valuation Uncertainty in Land Value Tax Simulation
abstract: Research supports that shifting property tax burdens from buildings to land values encourages development and improves equity (Cord, 1985). However, an analysis of these shifts depends on how land and improvement values are assessed. The Cook County Assessor's Office employs LightGBM to estimate parcel assessed values based on property characteristics, but this is only one modeling choice among many. This paper examines how alternative prediction models yield systematically different distributions of assessed value, and consequently different estimates of who gains and who loses under a tax shift. By comparing model predictions and the shape of their resulting distributions, we demonstrate that model selection is a first-order consideration in tax shift analysis, one that existing policy studies largely overlook. In this study, we examine how different machine learning (ML) predictions affect the analysis of a simulated transition from a Uniform Tax to a Land Value Tax (LVT). We find that because different ML models capture distinct underlying data structures, the predictions of the assessed parcel values vary, and downstream Uniform-to-LVT simulations yield significantly different outcomes across different metrics used to analyze the shift. These findings underscore the critical need for careful model selection. We caution that future analyses of tax simulations must explicitly account for the predictive variances and inherent limitations of the underlying machine learning models.
why: ML on property tax valuation, not financial trading or investment.

title: The Productivity Paradox Revisited: Generative AI, Skill Compression, and the Case for Complementary Human Capital Investment
abstract: The dominant narrative around generative artificial intelligence in the workplace holds that it raises productivity. This is true but incomplete, and the incompleteness matters for how firms should invest. Drawing on Brynjolfsson, Li, and Raymond's (2025) landmark field study of 5,172 customer support agentspublished in the Quarterly Journal of Economicsthis paper argues that generative AI's central economic signature is not productivity growth per se but skill compression: a 34-35 percent productivity gain concentrated almost entirely among novice and low-skill workers, alongside a small but measurable quality decline among the most experienced workers who used the tool. This pattern runs contrary to the skill-biased technical change that characterized prior waves of computerization, in which new technology systematically favored already-high-skill workers. We argue this reversal has direct implications for firm-level human capital strategy, and propose a reframing of AI capital investment decisions around workforce composition rather than aggregate productivity forecasts alone.
why: General AI workplace productivity, off-topic for financial ML.

title: AI and ESG Disclosure in Indian Listed Companies | Submission-oriented draft ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE AND THE QUALITY OF ESG DISCLOSURE: EVIDENCE FROM INDIAN LISTED COMPANIES
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly embedded in corporate decision systems, risk management, analytics, customer processes and sustainability management, while investors and regulators are simultaneously demanding more comparable and decision-useful environmental, social and governance (ESG) information. This study develops and tests an integrated model explaining how AI capability can influence the quality of ESG disclosure by strengthening firms' ESG data-analytics capability. It further examines whether board technology governance conditions the AI-ESG disclosure relationship. The empirical architecture is designed for Indian listed companies because the Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI) has progressively institutionalised quantitative sustainability reporting through the Business Responsibility and Sustainability Report (BRSR), with mandatory BRSR reporting for the top 1,000 listed entities from financial year 2022-23 and a phased BRSR Core assurance regime thereafter. The model conceptualises AI capability as a higher-order construct comprising strategic AI orientation, AI applications, AI investment, AI governance and AI-related human capital; ESG disclosure quality is modelled as a higher-order construct capturing environmental, social and governance disclosure quality, with emphasis on completeness, comparability, verifiability and decision usefulness. ESG data-analytics capability is specified as a mediator and board technology governance as a moderator. A SmartPLS-based higher-order PLS-SEM design, complemented by panel fixed-effects and robustness tests, is proposed. A 120 firm-year synthetic pilot dataset is supplied solely to demonstrate the analytical workflow; its illustrative results indicate positive direct and mediated associations and provide benchmark diagnostics for the final archival study. The principal contribution is a transparent, India-specific empirical framework linking AI capability with the quality-not merely the volumeof ESG disclosure under an evolving regulatory regime.
why: Single-country ESG study without transferable method or finance focus.

title: AI Life A Mother-agent Architecture for Heritable, Lifelong and Evolutionary Agentic Systems From Platform Competition to Governed Agent Lineages, with Financial-Market Applications
abstract: Working-paper notice. This paper develops a conceptual architecture and reports preliminary simulations. It does not claim that artificial agents are biologically alive or conscious, and it does not report deployment in a live financial institution. Product and company names, where mentioned, are illustrative context only. The views are the author's own and do not represent any employer or client.
why: Conceptual architecture, preliminary sims, explicitly no financial deployment.

title: Digital Transformation in African Accounting and Finance: Opportunities, Challenges and Future Prospects
abstract: Digital transformation is reshaping the methods, processes, and practical relevance of accounting and finance across Africa. Emerging technologies, including artificial intelligence, cloud accounting, blockchain, financial technology platforms, robotic process automation, big data analytics, electronic tax administration, and digital payment systems, are transforming bookkeeping, financial reporting, auditing, fraud detection, tax compliance, payment settlement, risk management, and financial decision-making. This paper examines the implications, opportunities, and constraints of digital transformation in accounting and finance across Africa, with comparative insights from Europe, North America, Asia-Pacific, Latin America, and the Middle East/Arab region. The study adopts a qualitative, conceptual, and integrative literature review design, employing thematic synthesis and cross-regional comparison of peer-reviewed studies, professional publications, and institutional reports. Evidence from selected African countries, including Nigeria, Kenya, Ghana, South Africa, Zimbabwe, Ethiopia, Uganda, and Tanzania, is examined to identify country-specific patterns, constraints, and opportunities.The findings indicate that digital transformation can enhance accounting efficiency, reporting timeliness, financial inclusion, audit analytics, transparency, and strategic financial capability. However, outcomes across Africa remain uneven due to infrastructure deficits, unreliable electricity, limited broadband access, high data costs, cybersecurity vulnerabilities, regulatory uncertainty, digital skills gaps, and inadequate organisational readiness. The paper concludes that Africa's digital accounting and finance transformation requires an integrated institutional, infrastructural, professional, technological, and governance approach. It contributes an Africa-focused digital accounting and finance transformation framework and proposes directions for future empirical research and policy development.
why: Qualitative literature review; rejected survey category.

title: Predictive Analytics and Digital Twin Integration for Construction Supply Chain Risk Management in Megaprojects: An Empirical Framework and Governance Model
abstract: Construction megaprojects are chronically impaired by multi-tier supply chain vulnerabilities, systemic logistical friction, and cascading schedule overruns that trigger multi-million-dollar disputes and severe commercial claims. Conventional construction supply chain risk management (CSCRM) relies almost exclusively on static, qualitative risk registers compiled during pre-tender planning, infrequent monthly audits, and retrospective Critical Path Method (CPM) progress updates in Oracle Primavera P6. These legacy mechanisms are fundamentally reactive; they detect procurement disruptions only after site delivery milestones have failed, leaving project controls teams with depleted float, exorbitant acceleration costs, and prolonged delay exposures. To resolve this structural operational bottleneck, this study develops, mathematically formulates, and empirically validates an end-to-end framework titled the Predictive Supply Chain Risk Governance (PSCRG) model. The PSCRG framework establishes a continuous cyber-physical feedback loop integrating multimodal enterprise telemetry-spanning 4D/5D Building Information Modeling (BIM), Internet of Things (IoT) logistical sensors, automated Automatic Identification System (AIS) vessel tracking, enterprise resource planning (ERP) financials, and Primavera P6 CPM logic-with high-dimensional machine learning and Dynamic Bayesian Belief Networks (BBN). The predictive core incorporates Extreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost), Light Gradient Boosting Machine (LightGBM), and Bidirectional Long Short-Term Memory (BiLSTM) recurrent neural networks to generate calibrated, asymmetric quantile distributions of material lead-time variance (Q_tau) and evaluate sub-tier vendor insolvency probabilities (P(Def)). Predicted supply shocks are mapped directly onto the project schedule network DAG to quantify dynamic critical path float dissipation, schedule elasticity (eta_SC), and downstream delay propagation. The framework incorporates an automated contractual governance engine grounded in FIDIC (1999/2017) and NEC4 standard forms, triggering verifiable Advance Warning Notices and optimizing proactive mitigation interventions via a Mixed-Integer Linear Programming (MILP) cost-loss optimization protocol. The PSCRG architecture was empirically deployed and validated across a longitudinal 48-month dataset from a completed $1.2 billion multi-facility infrastructure and high-rise complex megaproject encompassing 12,450 CPM activities, 42 primary contractors, and 18 highly critical, long-lead procurement packages. The stacking ensemble predictive model demonstrated superior forecasting accuracy over traditional CPM and linear baselines, achieving a Mean Absolute Error (MAE) of 5.8 calendar days (Mean Absolute Percentage Error [MAPE] of 3.84%) on lead times exceeding 180 days, and an Area Under the Receiver Operating Characteristic curve (AUC-ROC) of 0.952 in identifying vendor delivery distress. The framework detected upstream delivery failures an average of 54.2 calendar days prior to conventional monthly schedule updates, preserved 34.8% of available critical path float, and avoided an estimated $18.4 million in liquidated ascertained damages (LADs) and contractor prolongation overheads. This study bridges the long-standing divide between computational data science, critical path schedule analytics, and enforceable megaproject contractual governance.
why: Construction supply chain management; off-topic for finance.

title: Human-Centered Explainability in Insurance Claims Decision-Making: A Systematic Review of SHAP-Based Approaches and Their Effects on Analyst Trust and Decision Accuracy
abstract: Machine learning models increasingly inform high-stakes decisions in health and property-casualty insurance claims processing, yet their opacity creates a fundamental tension between predictive performance and the need for transparent, auditable, and human-contestable outcomes. This systematic review synthesizes 87 peer-reviewed studies published between 2017 and 2025 that examine SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations) as a mechanism for human-centered explainability in claims-related and adjacent decision-support contexts. We organize the literature around four analytical themes: (1) the technical properties of SHAP that make it attractive for regulated domains, (2) empirical evidence on how SHAP explanations affect human trust calibration, (3) effects on decision accuracy and appropriate reliance, and (4) documented risks of overreliance and explanation-induced bias. Our synthesis finds that SHAP explanations consistently improve perceived transparency and user confidence, but evidence for improved decision accuracy is weak, mixed, and highly context-dependent. We identify three critical gaps: the near-absence of studies conducted with actual claims analysts on real claims workflows, the lack of standardized trust and reliance measures across studies, and insufficient attention to how explanation presentation interacts with analyst expertise. We conclude with a research agenda and a methodological blueprint for a human-subjects study evaluating SHAP-based explanations in operational claims decision-making.
why: Systematic review of SHAP; rejected literature review category.
